When the UE experiences deteriorating signal conditions from the serving eNodeB, it sends a measurement report indicating that a neighbor cell is stronger. The serving eNodeB makes a handover decision and attempts to prepare the target eNodeB. However, if the target eNodeB cannot admit the UE due to lack of resources, it sends a Handover Preparation Failure message back to the source eNodeB.

During the initial access, the UE needs to transition from RRC_IDLE to RRC_CONNECTED. It starts by sending an RRC Connection Request. The network responds with an RRC Connection Setup message, establishing the SRB1. Finally, the UE confirms the successful establishment by sending the RRC Connection Setup Complete message.

The 5G system architecture consists of several key network functions. The AMF handles connection and mobility management, while the SMF is responsible for session management. The UPF routes and forwards user plane data. These functions interact via service-based interfaces to provide end-to-end connectivity for the UE.

To establish a dedicated bearer for a specific QoS flow, the network initiates the process. The MME sends a Bearer Setup Request to the eNodeB, which in turn sends an RRC Connection Reconfiguration message to the UE. The UE applies the new configuration and responds with an RRC Connection Reconfiguration Complete message.

In 5G NR, the gNB can be split into a Central Unit (CU) and one or more Distributed Units (DUs). The CU handles higher layer protocols like RRC and PDCP, while the DU handles lower layers like RLC, MAC, and PHY. They communicate over the F1 interface, allowing for flexible deployment scenarios.

When the network needs to reach a UE in CM-IDLE state, the AMF initiates a paging procedure. It sends a Paging message to all gNBs within the UE's tracking area. The gNBs broadcast the Paging message over the radio interface. Upon receiving the page, the UE initiates the RRC connection establishment procedure to transition to CM-CONNECTED state.

If the UE detects a radio link failure, it starts a timer and attempts to re-establish the connection. It selects a suitable cell and sends an RRC Reestablishment Request. If the network has the UE context, it responds with an RRC Reestablishment message. Otherwise, the re-establishment fails, and the UE goes to RRC_IDLE.

The LTE user plane protocol stack consists of several layers between the UE and the eNodeB. The Packet Data Convergence Protocol (PDCP) handles IP header compression and ciphering. The Radio Link Control (RLC) handles segmentation and reassembly. The Medium Access Control (MAC) handles multiplexing and HARQ. The Physical layer (PHY) handles modulation and coding.

To execute an Xn handover in 5G, the source NG-RAN node sends a Handover Request to the target NG-RAN node over the Xn interface. The target node performs admission control and responds with a Handover Request Acknowledge, including the RRC configuration for the UE. The source node then sends the Handover Command to the UE.

The random access procedure in LTE consists of four steps. First, the UE transmits a preamble (Msg1). The eNodeB responds with a Random Access Response (Msg2) containing an uplink grant. The UE transmits its RRC Connection Request (Msg3) using the grant. Finally, the eNodeB sends a Contention Resolution message (Msg4).

During the NAS authentication and key agreement procedure, the MME sends an Authentication Request to the UE containing a random challenge (RAND) and an authentication token (AUTN). The UE verifies the AUTN to authenticate the network. It then computes a response (RES) and sends it back in an Authentication Response message.

When the eNodeB detects that a UE has been inactive for a certain period, it can initiate the S1 release procedure to free up resources. It sends a UE Context Release Request to the MME. The MME asks the SGW to release the access bearers. Then, the MME sends a UE Context Release Command to the eNodeB, which releases the RRC connection and responds with a Complete message.

The mobility management entity (MME) manages the UE's state. When a UE is powered on, it is in the EMM-DEREGISTERED state. After a successful attach procedure, it transitions to EMM-REGISTERED. Within the registered state, the UE can be either in ECM-IDLE (no NAS signaling connection) or ECM-CONNECTED (active NAS signaling connection).

When a UE moves out of 5G coverage into an LTE coverage area, an inter-system handover from 5GS to EPS may be triggered. The source AMF communicates with the target MME over the N26 interface to transfer the UE context and prepare the target eNodeB. If the N26 interface is not supported, the UE must perform a registration procedure in the new system.

During a network-triggered service request, the network has downlink data for a UE in IDLE mode. The UPF notifies the SMF, which informs the AMF. The AMF pages the UE. The UE responds with a Service Request message. The network then establishes the necessary user plane resources and delivers the downlink data.
